title: Describe and represent objects in terms of shape, space and measurement

lessons.title: Shapes and space around the stable yard
lessons.html:
Flat shapes

Flat shapes have length and width but no thickness. You see them in the stable yard every day:

  • Square - 4 equal sides, 4 square corners. Many stables are square, for example 3.6 m by 3.6 m.
  • Rectangle - 4 sides, opposite sides equal, 4 square corners. A riding arena or a camp is often a rectangle.
  • Triangle - 3 sides. The roof end of a barn.
  • Circle - round, every point the same distance from the middle. A lunge ring or a round water trough.

Solid (3-D) shapes

Solid shapes have length, width and height.

ShapeFarm example
CubeA square box of salt licks
Rectangular box (cuboid)A small hay bale, a feed bin
CylinderA round bale, a water tank, a drum
ConeA pile of sand or a traffic cone at the arena

Position and direction

We use words to say where things are: left, right, in front of, behind, next to, between, above, below. For example: "The feed room is next to stable 4, behind the tack room."

A compass gives directions: north, south, east and west. In South Africa the sun rises in the east and sets in the west. At midday it is to the north.

Reading a simple plan

A plan is a drawing of a place seen from above. A yard plan shows stables as small rectangles, the arena as a big rectangle and the lunge ring as a circle. A key explains what each symbol means. A scale tells you how big things really are, for example 1 cm on the plan = 2 m on the ground.

Example: on the plan, the path from the gate to the feed room is 5 cm. With the scale 1 cm = 2 m, the real path is 5 × 2 = 10 m.

lessons.title: Measuring on the farm
lessons.html:
Units of measurement

What we measureUnitsFarm example
Lengthmillimetre (mm), centimetre (cm), metre (m), kilometre (km)Fence, stable wall, distance to town
Mass (weight)gram (g), kilogram (kg)Feed, a bag of cubes
Volume of liquidmillilitre (ml), litre (l)Water in a bucket, fly spray
Timeminutes, hours, daysExercise time, feeding times
Temperaturedegrees Celsius (°C)A horse's temperature, the weather

Remember: 10 mm = 1 cm, 100 cm = 1 m, 1 000 m = 1 km, 1 000 g = 1 kg, 1 000 ml = 1 l.

Perimeter

Perimeter is the distance all the way around a shape. You need it to know how much fencing or tape you need.

A camp is 40 m long and 25 m wide. Perimeter = 40 + 25 + 40 + 25 = 130 m. If the fence has 3 strands of wire, you need 3 × 130 = 390 m of wire.

Area

Area is the space inside a flat shape. We measure it in square metres (m²). For a rectangle: area = length × width.

A stable is 4 m by 3.5 m. Area = 4 × 3.5 = 14 m². This helps you know how much bedding or rubber matting to buy.

Volume

Volume is the space inside a solid. For a box shape: volume = length × width × height. A feed bin 1 m by 0.5 m by 0.8 m holds 1 × 0.5 × 0.8 = 0.4 m³.

Measuring tools

  • Tape measure - stables, fences, horse height
  • Scale - feed and medicine
  • Measuring jug - liquids
  • Thermometer - temperature
  • Weight tape - estimates a horse's weight from around the girth

Measure carefully

Start the tape at zero. Keep it straight and tight. Measure twice. Write the answer with its unit, for example 14 m², not just 14. A wrong measurement can mean too little wire, or the wrong amount of feed.

Key points

  • Know flat shapes (square, rectangle, triangle, circle) and solids (cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone).
  • A plan shows a place from above; use the scale to find real sizes.
  • Perimeter is the distance around; area is length × width.
  • Volume of a box is length × width × height.
  • Always write the unit and measure twice.
